executive_summary: EUR/GBP closed at 0.8498 on 2026-10-02 (pounds per euro; a rising pair means a stronger euro). That is one session after the 2026-10-01 valuation date, and every level in this report is anchored to it. The pair is down 1.15% over one month, 0.53% over three, 2.40% over six and 2.25% over twelve. It sits at the 8th percentile of its 52-week closing range (0.84671–0.88308), below a bearishly stacked set of 50/100/200-day averages and fractionally under an 11-touch band (0.84986–0.8577) that it has just broken out of. The bilateral story is two fiscal-stress episodes running at once. A French OAT-Bund widening with no TPI backstop hits the euro leg. A 28 October UK Budget that sterling spot has not priced, but options have, hits the pound. Underneath both, the energy shock, the dollar and the rise in long-end yields hit both legs alike and largely cancel. The settled first-pass verdict is Neutral on both horizons at conviction 1, with net scores of −0.0288 tactically and +0.0516 strategically. The bank consensus clusters at 0.86–0.88, above spot, so the verdict is a deliberate decision not to pay for the consensus long-EUR/GBP Budget trade. The caveat is that information arriving after the verdict was scored leans the near-term fundamental risk toward a lower pair: the OAT-Bund spread was briefly above 150bp on Friday. This report states that disagreement without re-scoring. The chart is used only for levels, sizing and the event map. It shows a range trapped between thin support near the July low and 32 touches of overhead supply within 280 pips.

market_context.valuation_assessment: On the REER-relative proxy that both dossiers use (BIS broad real, August 2026), the euro at 103.34 is about 8.0% cheap to sterling at 112.33. Applied to current spot, the ratio of 1.087 implies a valuation level near 0.92. This is a structural reading, not a PPP calculation, and it has no tactical trigger. A gap that size is the long-run reason a bank consensus sits above spot, and it is the substance behind the verdict's strategic Bullish Factor 5. It has not stopped the pair falling 2.40% in six months, because sovereign spreads and rate pricing are what currently set the cross. Crédit Agricole makes the opposite valuation point from a different angle: in its view 'The GBP no longer looks cheap vs the EUR based on relative real rate differential and relative sovereign credit risk spread'. Pricing currently reflects real-rate and credit-spread differentials, not REER. (Range shown on a closing basis, 0.84671–0.88308, percentile 8; the intraday range is 0.84536–0.88651 with spot at the 11th percentile. Spot is 31 pips above the lowest close of the year (15 July) and 381 pips below the highest; the last five sessions did most of the damage, with a 112 pip (−1.29%) fall from the 24 September close of 0.86092, and 0.8498 is the lowest close since 16 July (0.8489).)

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The policy differential is -125bp against the euro: ECB deposit rate 2.50% against Bank Rate 3.75%, both as supplied in the gated rate block. The live 10-year gap is about -184bp (gilt 5.42% against Bund 3.58%), and the quote dossier notes it has not moved over the month because Bunds and gilts sold off together. The gated monthly yields (-180.9bp as of 2026-08-01) are stale and are not used as live levels. What matters tactically is the surprise relative to pricing, and both legs carry dovish-surprise risk. Almost 80% of a 25bp BoE hike on 5 November is priced, with 39bp priced to December. So a delivered hike does nothing for sterling, while a hold would push EUR/GBP higher. The ECB hike probability for 29 October had dropped below 30% by 30 September. Then the 2 October flash HICP came in at 3.8% against 3.6% expected, with core at 2.5%. That reopens the October debate and challenges Lagarde's view that long yields are doing part of the tightening. The ECB decides on 29 October, a week before the BoE's Monetary Policy Report meeting on 5 November, so the euro side resolves first. The BoE meeting carries the projection round and is the higher-stakes date. The two asymmetries roughly cancel, so carry is the only one-sided element, and carry by itself is not a direction.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the two dossiers' base cases leave the differential roughly where it is now. The quote dossier expects one BoE hike to 4.00% and a stop, about 14bp short of the curve's implied path to December. The base dossier expects one ECB hike, most likely on 17 December with staff projections, against a German front end pricing about 70bp over two years. Over the strategic horizon both curves therefore look modestly too hawkish by similar amounts. The September HICP beat makes ECB under-delivery less likely than the base dossier assumed, because it came with services rising to 3.2% and core to 2.5%. Both banks decide on 17 December. That same-day clustering means relative repricing will happen in one session rather than drifting, and the ECB meeting carries the projection round. Two caps work in opposite directions. French spreads limit how far the ECB can go, and a softening UK labour market (payrolled employees down 101,000 on the year, regular pay slowing to 3.5%) limits the BoE. Neither cap clearly dominates, so the factor stays Neutral, slightly less confident than tactically.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Recent data surprises favour the euro side. The euro-area September flash put headline HICP at 3.8% against 3.6% expected, the highest since September 2023. Core was 2.5% and services rose to 3.2% from 3.0%, so the acceleration was not purely energy, and commentators read it as making Lagarde's patience harder to sustain before 29 October. Euro-area activity is also beating: the September flash composite PMI was 53.1 against 51.7 expected, a 41-month high. On the UK side, August CPI rose to 3.1%, but core (2.6%) and services (3.4%) were unchanged, and the September flash composite PMI fell to 51.7 from 52.5. The UK's offset is growth: Q2 GDP was revised up and commentators link that to sterling support and BoE room to hike. On net, the euro area has the upside surprise in both inflation breadth and survey momentum, and it is the side whose central bank is priced least for a reaction. That is how this factor moves the pair over four weeks. The swing prints are euro-area final HICP on 16 October and UK September CPI on 21 October.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months both economies face the same real-income squeeze from imported energy, and neither has a clear relative advantage. In the UK, the January Ofgem cap is forecast 16% higher against real regular pay growth of about +0.6%, and the labour market is softening: payrolls down 101,000 on the year, vacancies at 702,000 and a claimant count beat to the upside. In the euro area, negotiated wages slowed to 3.0%, German consumer confidence is very weak at -30.6, and gas storage is about 12 points below a year ago going into winter. Growth runs at similar rates, 1.4% year on year in the UK and 1.2% in the euro area, with ECB staff at 0.9% for 2026. The euro area has a fiscal growth cushion the UK lacks: Germany's 2027 draft budget raises spending 5.9% with an investment ratio above 10%. The UK's shorter mortgage fixations mean BoE hikes reach household demand faster. Both central banks are hiking into stagflationary supply shocks, and the differential in growth and inflation momentum is too small and too uncertain to carry a strategic stance.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: EUR/GBP is classified as a low risk-sensitivity pair, and the current regime does not give the usual risk-off read. The textbook pattern, where sterling as the more risk-sensitive leg weakens in equity drawdowns and lifts the cross, is overridden by a global long-end duration shock. That shock hits both legs through their sovereign markets. On the UK side, the 30-year gilt touched 6% for the first time since 1998, and ING notes sterling is more sensitive than the euro or the dollar to long-end bond sell-offs. On the euro side, French OATs moved above 4.9%, and ING described 2 October as showing the first signs of broader contagion into Italian, Greek and Belgian spreads. Equity volatility is low (VIX about 16) and the signal is in credit (US high yield 42bp wider on the month). So the transmission into this pair runs through sovereign spreads, not equity beta, and both legs are exposed. With duration stress on both sides and no clear haven between them, the factor does not lean either way.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the main risk branches affect both legs together. An Iran settlement that normalised LNG and refined-product flows would ease gas prices for both net energy importers. The euro area would gain somewhat more through TTF and storage, and the UK through the Ofgem cap, so the net is close to zero. Renewed Hormuz closure would hurt both. A disorderly French spread episode is the one euro-specific risk-off branch, and a post-Budget gilt dislocation is the sterling-specific one. The quote dossier's crisis correlation (gilts and sterling falling together) and the base dossier's lack of TPI cover for fundamentals-driven French widening describe mirror-image tails. No observable cross-asset variable separates them over the horizon, so the honest stance is Neutral with low confidence.

The euro area's July current account missed at EUR27.6bn against EUR30.7bn expected, down from EUR35.1bn, as EU energy imports rose 13.9% year on year to EUR41.3bn. Both are net energy importers, and both of the framework's commodity rules point the same way for each leg: oil up is negative for EUR and GBP, and TTF/gas up is negative for EUR and GBP. So the commodity channel nets close to zero for the cross. Monthly trade releases inside four weeks rarely move a cross with this little vol, and the factor's tactical weight is only 0.06.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Structurally, the external accounts and real valuation both favour the euro against sterling. The euro area runs a current account surplus of 1.92% of GDP (2026-Q1 vintage) against a UK deficit of 2.5%. The UK's primary income account has swung to a GBP3.8bn quarterly deficit as payments to foreign holders of UK assets outgrow receipts, which is the external cost of funding a 93.8%-of-GDP debt at 5%-plus yields with 25-30% of gilts held abroad. Bilaterally, IMF DOTS shows the euro area exported USD312.0bn of goods to the UK in 2024 against USD158.4bn of imports, a USD153.6bn surplus with its largest trading partner after the US. The UK's mirror data (USD196.0bn exports, USD345.0bn imports) confirm the direction. On a REER-relative proxy (BIS broad real, August 2026), the euro at 103.34 is about 8% cheap to sterling at 112.33. Sterling's high carry has already been capitalised into its real exchange rate, while the euro has not appreciated in real terms despite two hikes. The offsets are real: the euro area's energy deficit is widening and storage is thin, and the UK services surplus of GBP51.3bn is growing. Over one to three months, the surplus-versus-deficit gap and the valuation gap tilt the cross higher at moderate confidence.

The euro's cheapness and its surplus are not being rewarded. That gap closes slowly, which is why this is a strategic tilt and not a tactical one.

net_commodity_exposure.base_commodity_profile: Euro area is a large net importer of oil and gas, with EU energy imports EUR41.3bn a month; most exposed to TTF gas (EUR72.90/MWh, 43% above the ECB's EUR51.0 assumption) with storage about 70%, roughly 12 points below a year earlier.
net_commodity_exposure.quote_commodity_profile: UK is a net energy importer with declining North Sea output and limited storage; most exposed to NBP gas (182.89p/therm, +128.58% y/y), which passes through to households via the Ofgem cap, forecast +16% in January.
net_commodity_exposure.net_effect_calculation: Step 1, oil: rule says oil up means -EUR and -GBP; both are importers of similar intensity, so the net pair effect is about zero. Step 2, gas (TTF/NBP): rule says TTF up means -EUR and -GBP. The euro area's thinner storage buffer raises its sensitivity, while the UK's limited storage and the Ofgem pass-through raise sterling's real-income sensitivity. Call it a small net negative for EUR, partly offset by the UK cap mechanism. Step 3, net: a commodity shock moves both legs the same way, and any residual is too small and uncertain to sign. Energy is therefore not a directional driver of EUR/GBP, unlike EUR/NOK or GBP/NOK.
net_commodity_exposure.scenario_oil_up_10pct: Both legs weaken against exporters (NOK, CAD); net EUR/GBP impact about zero, with possibly a slight fall if refined-product costs bite the euro area's larger energy deficit first.
net_commodity_exposure.scenario_oil_down_10pct: Both legs gain against exporters; net EUR/GBP impact about zero; a settlement-driven move that also eases gas would help both, with no clear net sign.
net_commodity_exposure.dominant_commodity_driver: European/UK natural gas (TTF and NBP), which moves both legs the same way and so explains little of EUR/GBP's direction.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The two central banks' guidance points in opposite directions. The MPC moved pricing to almost 80% for a November hike without moving rates: three members voted for 4.00% on 17 September, the Bank projects CPI 'slightly over 4% in early 2027', and Deputy Governor Lombardelli, a hold voter, said policy is increasingly likely to need to tighten if energy prices persist. The ECB has said it is not pre-committing. Lagarde described a 'measured response' on a 'middle path', told Parliament on 30 September that the ECB does not react to energy prices as such, and signalled that higher long yields are doing some of the tightening. Even Schnabel framed further moves as conditional. A hawk-leaning MPC against a deliberately non-committal ECB means communication into the 29 October and 5 November meetings is weighted toward sterling. Two things hold confidence down. The 2 October inflation beat makes Lagarde's patience harder to defend. And the BoE has internal dissonance: Taylor publicly downplayed the case for an energy-driven hike, and the 5 November MPR conditions its forecast on market rates, which could itself read as dovish.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months, credibility is intact at both banks, and each one's guidance carries a specific weakness that offsets the other's. The BoE publishes individual votes, so its hawk-dove arithmetic is visible. But the Committee spoke with two voices within one week, under-forecast August CPI by 30bp, and its MPR convention can turn its own forecast into a dovish signal. Both projection rounds fall inside the horizon: the BoE MPR on 5 November and ECB staff projections on 17 December. Each is where the respective guidance either holds or gives way. This factor is kept Neutral to avoid counting the curve-versus-rhetoric gap twice, since Factor 1 already scores relative pricing. On communications alone, neither bank is more likely to disappoint than the other.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Each leg has its own political event risk, and they pull the cross in opposite directions. For sterling, the 28 October Budget is the largest dated binary in the window. The OBR's March headroom has been largely consumed by higher yields, it is the first Budget of a new administration, and EUR/GBP options are positioned for sterling downside. For the euro, the French 2027 budget presented on 1 October was met by a sharp widening in OAT-Bund. ING called the 2 October move the first signs of broader contagion, and a minority government needs parliamentary approval, with the vote on 17 November falling just beyond the tactical window. Both events affect the shared Iran/energy risk only indirectly. The UK binary lands inside the window but is hedged in options; the French stress is live in spot bond markets now. The two event exposures are of similar size and opposite sign.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the political calendar leans against the euro. The UK's main binary resolves on 28 October, and the governing party has no general election due before 2029, so residual UK political risk is slow-moving (the remit revision, the Ofgem cap). The euro area's runs longer. The French budget faces a 17 November vote after France has had three governments in fourteen months. Polling for the 2027 presidential race puts populist candidates in the lead, which feeds directly into the OAT risk premium. Spanish and Italian elections also fall in 2027, and Italy's 2025 deficit was 3.1% of GDP. Transmission into EUR/GBP runs through euro-area sovereign risk premia and real-money euro allocation. The one large two-sided branch, an Iran settlement, affects both energy importers similarly, so it does not offset the asymmetric political calendar.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Both sovereigns are under stress, but over the next four weeks the more acute and less backstopped stress is French. OAT-Bund widened by about 13bp in one session to 130.3bp on 1 October, against a one-year average near 75bp, and was reported above 140bp the next day. ING described 2 October as the first signs of broader contagion, with Italian two-year spreads nearly doubling in a session. French debt is 119.3% of GDP rising to 121.7%. The ECB's TPI is designed for disorderly, unwarranted dynamics, not fundamentals-driven widening, so there is no mechanical ceiling. On the UK side, the 30-year gilt has touched 6%, August borrowing overshot the OBR by GBP3.5bn and headroom has been largely consumed. But the Chancellor has said fiscal discipline will be at the core of the Budget and that the rules will be met, and UK debt is 93.8% of GDP and slightly lower year on year. The counterweight is ING's observation that sterling carries no fiscal risk premium, which leaves sterling more exposed to repricing on 28 October. On balance, the stress already in motion is French, and it transmits to EUR/GBP through euro risk premia.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months both fiscal problems are chronic, and each has an offset. France's debt path and political fragmentation are durable negatives. Germany's large, AAA-rated issuance (2027 net borrowing EUR118.7bn, investment ratio above 10%) supplies the safe asset the euro area lacks and partly offsets them. The UK's debt-service bill is rising with yields and RPI-linked uplift, and domestic DB pension demand for long gilts is declining. But UK debt/GDP is slightly lower on the year, all agencies hold AA-equivalent ratings with stable outlooks, and the Budget resolves the near-term uncertainty early. The euro area's stress is concentrated in one large member; the UK's is a single sovereign whose currency carries the full transmission. Neither dominates strategically.

tactical.rationale: The two dossiers' standalone views largely cancel in this cross. Both are Bearish on their own currency, and in each case the main driver is the dollar or a domestic fiscal problem, neither of which favours one leg over the other. The heaviest factor, Policy & Rates at 0.24, is Neutral. Sterling's 25bp November hike is almost 80% priced, so delivery is no news and a hold would lift the pair. The ECB's 29 October hike had been priced below 30% before a 3.8% September flash against 3.6% expected reopened it. Both legs carry dovish-surprise risk, and the -125bp carry is a cost of holding, not a direction. Inflation & Growth is the one positive: the euro area is beating on inflation breadth (services 3.2%, core 2.5%) and on surveys (composite 53.1 against the UK's 51.7). That is the data side whose central bank is less priced. Three small negatives outweigh it, and the bilateral factors that modify the standalone views sit here. First, positioning: the GBP spec short at -82,600 is far more stretched than the EUR short at -52,334, and EUR/GBP Budget-week options lean about three-quarters bearish on sterling, so the pair is implicitly crowded long. Second, guidance: a hawk-leaning MPC against an ECB that is deliberately not committing. Third, fiscal: France is the acute, unbackstopped sovereign stress, with OAT-Bund through 130bp on 1 October and contagion signs on 2 October. On what is priced against what we expect, sterling's fiscal risk is priced in options rather than spot, French risk is being priced in bonds now, and there is no clean edge. The path of least resistance is two-way and event-driven, not trending. The key dated catalysts are UK CPI on 21 October, the Budget and OBR on 28 October, the ECB on 29 October, the BoE MPR on 5 November, and the French vote on 17 November, just beyond the window. Conviction is 1 because the score is close to zero and its sign depends on two 52-confidence factors that could each turn on a single headline. || Pass-2 analyst note on the settled verdict (fundamental, not chart-based): Information that arrived after the verdict was scored leans the tactical fundamental risk toward a lower pair, though not by enough to change the stance here. The French spread kept widening after the verdict's 130–140bp references: French budget concerns pushed the OAT-Bund spread to 154 basis points. ING's rates team had already flagged that 150bp may be the next step for the 10yr OAT-Bund spread, and warned that the euro's correlation with eurozone spread widening can pick up rapidly. On the rate side, the ECB's October optionality appears to have narrowed rather than widened after the flash, with markets now pricing three ECB hikes over 12 months, down from four, and only a 20% chance in October. Had pass 1 seen these, Factor 8's tactical Bearish confidence of 52 and Factor 2's tactical Bullish confidence of 55 would both have been under pressure in the euro-negative direction. A Factor 8 confidence near 65 and a Factor 2 near 45 would have taken the tactical score to about −0.05: still Neutral by rule, but closer to the −0.10 line. The published view is therefore Neutral with a stated near-term skew toward the lower half of the range. The verdict stands as issued.

strategic.score_interpretation: A net score of +0.0516 is inside the Neutral band, so the stance is Neutral by rule. Only two factors carry a non-zero contribution. External Balance & Terms of Trade at +0.088 reflects the euro's current-account surplus against the UK's deficit, its USD153.6bn bilateral goods surplus and an 8% real-valuation gap in the euro's favour. Event Risk at -0.0364 reflects a euro political calendar that runs longer than the UK's. Eight factors, including the heaviest (Policy & Rates), are Neutral. The slight positive tilt depends on a slow-moving structural factor and is not strong enough to justify a stance.
strategic.rationale: At strategic weights the heaviest factors are Neutral. On Policy & Rates, both curves look modestly too hawkish against their dossiers' base cases: one BoE hike on 5 November and one ECB hike on 17 December would leave the gap near -125bp. Guidance is Neutral because both banks are credible and each projection round (BoE MPR 5 November, ECB staff projections 17 December) can undercut its own curve. The structural positive is External Balance at a 0.16 weight. The euro area runs a 1.92%-of-GDP surplus against a UK deficit of 2.5%. The UK's primary income deficit is widening as it funds a 93.8%-of-GDP debt at 5%-plus yields. IMF DOTS shows a USD153.6bn euro-area goods surplus with the UK. And the euro is about 8% cheap to sterling on the BIS REER-relative proxy, because sterling's carry has already been capitalised into its real exchange rate. Event Risk offsets part of that. The UK's main binary resolves on 28 October with no election before 2029, while France votes on 17 November and goes into a 2027 presidential race led by populist candidates, with Italian and Spanish elections also due. The dossiers conflict here: the quote dossier's strategic sterling bear case runs on terms of trade and fiscal risk, and the base dossier's euro bear case runs on energy and France. In this cross the energy shock hits both legs alike. What is priced against what we expect: the market has not priced sterling's external deficit into its currency, which is the edge, but that edge is slow. The path of least resistance is a range shaped by the 17 December double meeting. Conviction is 1 because the score is within 0.05 of zero and rests on one 55-confidence factor.
strategic.g10_relative_ranking: Strategically the base dossier ranks the euro 7th of 11 and the quote dossier ranks sterling 8th, so EUR/GBP pairs two mid-to-low-ranked currencies, and their bear cases largely cancel. Among euro crosses, EUR/SEK and EUR/CHF offer cleaner euro-long logic, and EUR/CAD a cleaner euro-short logic. Among sterling crosses, short GBP/NOK expresses the UK terms-of-trade thesis more purely than long EUR/GBP, because Norway is an energy exporter and the euro area is not.

Second, the ECB curve is also over-priced against the ECB's stated reaction function, so the BoE over-pricing argument applies to both legs.
